concepts: Direct common tangents and a circle through the points of contact; chord length of a circle
questions.question: Consider two circles in the Cartesian plane defined by $C_1:x^2+y^2=25$ and $C_2:x^2+y^2-10x+21=0$. Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be the two direct common tangents to the circles $C_1$ and $C_2$, where $L_1$ touches $C_1$ and $C_2$ at the points $P_1$ and $P_2$ respectively, and $L_2$ touches $C_1$ and $C_2$ at the points $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ respectively. Let $C_3$ be the unique circle passing through the four points of tangency $P_1,P_2,Q_1$ and $Q_2$. If the line $L:4x-3y=0$ intersects the circle $C_3$ at two distinct points $A$ and $B$, then the length of the chord $AB$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: By symmetry about the line of centres, the centre of $C_3$ lies on the $x$-axis, so one equal-distance equation fixes it.
solution: The external centre of similitude $T_e$ divides $O_1O_2$ externally in the ratio $5:2$: $T_e=\left(\frac{5(5)-2(0)}{5-2},0\right)=\left(\frac{25}{3},0\right)$.
So the direct common tangents are $L_1:3x-4y-25=0$ and $L_2:3x+4y-25=0$.
Points of contact on $C_1$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $(0,0)$ to $L_1,L_2$: $P_1=(3,-4)$, $Q_1=(3,4)$.
The four points are symmetric about the $x$-axis, so the centre of $C_3$ lies on the $x$-axis at $(x_0,0)$.
Equal distances from $(x_0,0)$ to $Q_1(3,4)$ and $Q_2\left(\frac{31}{5},\frac85\right)$: $(3-x_0)^2+16=\left(\frac{31}{5}-x_0\right)^2+\frac{64}{25}\Rightarrow x_0=\frac52$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Midpoint theorem on the right trapezoid $O_1P_1P_2O_2$ places the centre of $C_3$ at the midpoint of $O_1O_2$.
solution: $O_1P_1\perp L_1$ and $O_2P_2\perp L_1$, so $O_1P_1P_2O_2$ is a right trapezoid with parallel sides $5$ and $2$.
Projection on $L_1$ preserves midpoints: the perpendicular to $L_1$ through the midpoint $M$ of $O_1O_2$ passes through the midpoint of $P_1P_2$, so $MP_1=MP_2$.
In the same way $MQ_1=MQ_2$, and $MP_1=MQ_1$ by symmetry in the $x$-axis. So $C_3$ has centre $M=\left(\frac52,0\right)$.
Length of the direct tangent segment: $P_1P_2=\sqrt{(O_1O_2)^2-(R_1-R_2)^2}=\sqrt{25-9}=4$.
Distance of $M$ from $L_1$ is the mean of $5$ and $2$, i.e. $\frac72$.

useful_results: Two circles with radii $R_1,R_2$ and centre distance $d$: direct common tangent length $\sqrt{d^2-(R_1-R_2)^2}$, transverse length $\sqrt{d^2-(R_1+R_2)^2}$.
The external centre of similitude divides $O_1O_2$ externally in the ratio $R_1:R_2$; both direct common tangents pass through it.

The four points of contact of the two direct common tangents lie on a circle centred at the midpoint of $O_1O_2$ with $\rho^2=\frac{d^2+4R_1R_2}{4}$. Here: centre $\left(\frac52,0\right)$, $\rho^2=\frac{25+40}{4}=\frac{65}{4}$.
A chord at distance $p$ from the centre of a circle of radius $\rho$ has length $2\sqrt{\rho^2-p^2}$.

concepts: Non-differentiability of $f(x)=\max_{t\in[0,x]}g(t)$
Definite integral of a piecewise function
questions.question: Consider a function $g:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ defined non-uniformly by $g(t)=\begin{cases}4t-t^2, & 0\le t\le3\\ t^2-8t+18, & 3<t\le6\\ 4t-18, & t>6\end{cases}$. Let the function $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x)=\max_{t\in[0,x]}g(t)$. If $S$ denotes the set of all points in the open interval $(0,\infty)$ at which $f(x)$ is NOT differentiable, then which of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.key_idea: A running maximum is flat while $g$ is below its old peak and has a corner only where $g$ climbs back to that peak with non-zero slope.
solution: For $0\le t\le3$: $g'(t)=4-2t$ vanishes at $t=2$. So $g$ increases on $[0,2]$ from $g(0)=0$ to a local maximum $g(2)=4$, then decreases on $[2,3]$ to $g(3)=3$.
For $3<t\le6$: $g'(t)=2t-8$, so $g$ has a local minimum at $t=4$ with $g(4)=2$.
For $t\in(4,6]$, $g$ strictly increases to $g(6)=6$; for $t>6$, $g'(t)=4>0$, so $g$ strictly increases for all $t>6$.
The earlier peak $4$ is regained when $t^2-8t+18=4\Rightarrow t=4+\sqrt2$; until then $f(x)=4$ (flat) for $2<x<4+\sqrt2$.
At $x=2$: $\lim_{x\to2^-}f'(x)=4-2(2)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to2^+}f'(x)=0$. So $f$ is differentiable at $x=2$ with $f'(2)=0$.
At $x=6$: $\lim_{x\to6^-}f'(x)=2(6)-8=4$ and $\lim_{x\to6^+}f'(x)=4$. So $f$ is differentiable at $x=6$ with $f'(6)=4$.
At $x=4+\sqrt2$: the left derivative is $0$ while the right derivative is $2(4+\sqrt2)-8=2\sqrt2$, so $f$ is non-differentiable there.
Hence $S=\{4+\sqrt2\}$ and $f'(2)+f'(6)=0+4=4$: option (B). Options (A), (C), (D) all state a wrong set $S$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Graph view: $f$ follows $g$ at new records and stays flat otherwise, so smoothness is decided by $g'$ at the joins.
solution: $f$ equals $g$ while $g$ is setting a new maximum, and is constant while $g$ lies below the earlier peak.
Peak at $t=2$: $g(2)=4$ and $g'(2)=0$. A rising arc meeting a flat piece with the same slope $0$ gives no corner at $x=2$.
$g$ climbs back to height $4$ when $t^2-8t+14=0$, i.e. $t=4\pm\sqrt2$; only $t=4+\sqrt2$ lies on the branch $(3,6]$ ($4-\sqrt2<3$).
There $g'(4+\sqrt2)=2(4+\sqrt2)-8=2\sqrt2\neq0$ against slope $0$ of the flat piece: a corner, so $4+\sqrt2\in S$.
At $t=3$ the formula of $g$ changes but $g(3)=3<4$, so $f$ is flat there: no corner. At $t=6$ the branches $t^2-8t+18$ and $4t-18$ have equal values ($6$) and equal slopes ($4$): no corner.

useful_results: A running maximum $f(x)=\max_{[0,x]}g$ of a continuous $g$ is continuous and non-decreasing. It is non-differentiable only where $g$ regains its previous maximum with non-zero slope, or where a rising part of $g$ has a corner of its own.
$f'=g'$ where $g$ is at its running maximum and $f'=0$ where $f$ is flat. At a smooth peak $g'=0$, so the join is smooth.
For piecewise $g$, also test the joins of $g$ itself ($t=3,6$ here): equal values and equal slopes mean no corner.
Instance: $\int_0^4f(x)\,dx=\int_0^2(4x-x^2)dx+4\cdot2=\frac{16}{3}+8=\frac{40}{3}$ - option (C) has a true integral but a wrong $S$.

concepts: Radical centre and power of a point
Parabola as a locus (focus-directrix property)
questions.question: Consider two fixed circles $S_1:x^2+y^2-1=0$ and $S_2:x^2+y^2-6x+8=0$. Let $S_3$ be a variable circle passing through the point $(3,0)$ and touching the line $x+3=0$. Let $P$ be the radical centre of the circles $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$. If the power of the point $P$ with respect to the circle $S_1$ is minimum, then the length of the tangent drawn from $P$ to the circle $S_3$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: The radical centre moves on the fixed line $x=\frac32$, so its power w.r.t. $S_1$ is $\frac94-1+y_0^2$, least at $y_0=0$.
solution: The radical centre $P(x_0,y_0)$ lies on the radical axis of $S_1,S_2$: $S_1-S_2=0\Rightarrow6x-9=0\Rightarrow x_0=\frac32$.

Let the centre of $S_3$ be $(h,k)$. $S_3$ passes through $(3,0)$ and touches $x=-3$, so its centre lies on the parabola with focus $(3,0)$ and directrix $x=-3$: $(h-3)^2+k^2=(h+3)^2\Rightarrow k^2=12h$.
The radical axis of $S_1$ and $S_3$ ($S_1-S_3=0$) is $hx+ky-3h+4=0$.
For $k\neq0$, the $y$-coordinate of the radical centre is $y_0=\frac k8-\frac4k$.
The power is minimum when $y_0=0$, which gives $k^2=32$ (real $k$ exists). The minimum power w.r.t. $S_1$ (and so w.r.t. $S_3$) is $\frac54$.
Length of the tangent from $P$ to $S_3$: $\sqrt{\text{power}}=\sqrt{\frac54}=\frac{\sqrt5}{2}$: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Bound first, then show the bound is attained: $P$ lies on $x=\frac32$, so $OP\ge\frac32$ and the power $OP^2-1\ge\frac54$; an explicit circle $S_3$ attains it.
solution: $P$ lies on the radical axis $x=\frac32$ of $S_1,S_2$, and its power $p$ is the same w.r.t. all three circles.
Power w.r.t. $S_1$ (centre $O$, radius $1$) is $OP^2-1$, and $OP\ge\frac32$ for every point of $x=\frac32$. So $p\ge\frac94-1=\frac54$.
Attainment: take the centre $(h,k)=\left(\frac83,4\sqrt2\right)$, which is on $k^2=12h$ since $32=12\cdot\frac83$. Its radius is $h+3=\frac{17}{3}$.
Check: it passes through $(3,0)$ since $\left(3-\frac83\right)^2+32=\frac19+32=\frac{289}{9}=\left(\frac{17}{3}\right)^2$, and it touches $x=-3$ because its radius equals $h+3$.

For this $S_3$ the radical axis of $S_1,S_3$ is $hx+ky-3h+4=\frac83x+4\sqrt2\,y-4=0$, and $\left(\frac32,0\right)$ satisfies it ($4-4=0$). So $P=\left(\frac32,0\right)$ is the radical centre and $p=\frac54$ is attained.
Tangent length from $P$ to $S_3$ is $\sqrt p=\frac{\sqrt5}{2}$: option (A).

useful_results: The radical centre of three circles is the common point of the three radical axes; its power is the same for all three, and the tangent length from it to each circle is $\sqrt{\text{power}}$.
A circle through a fixed point $F$ touching a fixed line has its centre on the parabola with focus $F$ and directrix that line (radius = distance to the line = distance to $F$).
Radical axis of two circles: subtract their equations ($S_1-S_2=0$). Power of $(x_0,y_0)$ w.r.t. $x^2+y^2=r^2$ is $x_0^2+y_0^2-r^2$.
To minimise the power over a line of possible radical centres, take the point of that line nearest the centre of $S_1$, then check it is attainable.

concepts: Definite integral of a periodic function and estimation of integrals
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous periodic function with period $\pi$, defined by $f(x)=\frac{1}{1+\sin^2x}$ for all $x\in[0,\pi]$. Consider the definite integral $I=\int_0^{2026\pi}\frac{x^2f(x)}{1+x^2}\,dx$. Which of the following inequalities is satisfied by $I$?
questions.key_idea: Write $\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}=1-\frac1{1+x^2}$: the periodic part integrates exactly, the rest needs only bounds from $\frac12\le f\le1$.
solution: For the remaining part let $J=\int_0^{2026\pi}\frac{f(x)}{1+x^2}\,dx$. Since $0\le\sin^2x\le1$, we get $\frac12\le f(x)\le1$.
Hence $\frac{1}{2(1+x^2)}\le\frac{f(x)}{1+x^2}\le\frac{1}{1+x^2}$, and integrating (strictly, the bounds being met only at isolated points): $\frac12\tan^{-1}(2026\pi)<J<\tan^{-1}(2026\pi)$.
questions.correction_note: Step 4: the PDF writes $2\int_0^\infty\frac{1}{1+u^2}\frac{du}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2[\tan^{-1}u]_0^\infty$, which skips the substitution. The integrand after $u=\tan x$ is $\frac1{1+2u^2}$ (not $\frac1{1+u^2}$), and the value $\frac\pi{\sqrt2}$ needs $v=\sqrt2u$ (i.e. $\tan^{-1}(\sqrt2u)$). The final value $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt2}$ and the answer (A) are unchanged. Also the strictness of the bounds on $J$ is stated explicitly.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate by size first, then use the mean value of one period and the strict bound $f>\frac12$.
solution: Options (C) and (D) have lower bounds above $2026\sqrt2\pi-\frac\pi2\approx9000>6365$, so both are impossible.
$I=1013\sqrt2\pi-J$ with $J=\int_0^{2026\pi}\frac{f}{1+x^2}dx$. Since $f>\frac12$ except at isolated points, $J>\frac12\tan^{-1}(2026\pi)$, hence $I<1013\sqrt2\pi-\frac12\tan^{-1}(2026\pi)$.
Option (B) claims $I>1013\sqrt2\pi-\frac12\tan^{-1}(2026\pi)$, a contradiction; so only (A) remains (and $J<\tan^{-1}(2026\pi)$ gives its lower end).

useful_results: For $f$ periodic with period $T$: $\int_0^{nT}f(x)\,dx=n\int_0^Tf(x)\,dx$.
$\int_0^\pi\frac{dx}{a+b\sin^2x}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{a(a+b)}}$ for $a>0,\ a+b>0$. Here $a=b=1$ gives $\frac\pi{\sqrt2}$.

Split $\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}=1-\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ to separate an exactly integrable periodic part from a convergent tail, and bound the tail with $m\le f\le M$: $m\tan^{-1}b<\int_0^b\frac{f}{1+x^2}dx<M\tan^{-1}b$.
If $g\le h$ are continuous and not identically equal, then $\int g<\int h$ (strict inequality).

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Chord of contact, pole and polar, and loci in a circle
questions.question: Consider the circle $C:x^2+y^2=4$ and the straight line $L:3x+4y=25$. Let $P$ be a variable point lying on the line $L$. From $P$, a pair of tangents are drawn to the circle $C$, touching it at the points $A$ and $B$. Then which of the following statement(s) is (are) TRUE?
options: The chord of contact $AB$ always passes through the fixed point $\left(\frac{12}{25},\frac{16}{25}\right)$.
The locus of the circumcentre of $\triangle PAB$ is the line $6x+8y=25$.
The locus of the midpoint of the chord $AB$ is a circle passing through the origin.
The minimum length of the chord $AB$ occurs when $OP$ is perpendicular to the line $L$ (where $O$ is the origin).
questions.key_idea: The chord of contact $xx_1+yy_1=4$, with $P(x_1,y_1)$ on a line, is a family of lines through the pole of that line.
solution: The chord of contact $AB$ from $P(x_1,y_1)$ to the circle $C$ is $T=0$: $xx_1+yy_1=4$.
This family of lines passes through the intersection of $4x-3y=0$ and $25y-16=0$, i.e. the fixed point $\left(\frac{12}{25},\frac{16}{25}\right)$. (A) is true.

$\angle OAP=\angle OBP=90^\circ$, so $OAPB$ is cyclic and the circumcircle of $\triangle PAB$ has $OP$ as diameter. Its centre $M(h,k)$ is the midpoint of $OP$: $h=\frac{x_1}{2},\ k=\frac{y_1}{2}\Rightarrow x_1=2h,\ y_1=2k$.
Substituting in $3x_1+4y_1=25$: $3(2h)+4(2k)=25\Rightarrow6h+8k=25$. The locus is the line $6x+8y=25$. (B) is true.
Let $N(x_0,y_0)$ be the midpoint of $AB$. The chord with midpoint $N$ is $T=S_1$: $xx_0+yy_0=x_0^2+y_0^2$.
The locus $25(x^2+y^2)-12x-16y=0$ is a circle passing through the origin. (C) is true.
Let $d=OP$. The length of the chord of contact is $AB=\frac{2R\sqrt{d^2-R^2}}{d}=\frac{2(2)\sqrt{d^2-4}}{d}=4\sqrt{1-\frac{4}{d^2}}$.
$AB$ is least when $1-\frac4{d^2}$ is least, i.e. when $d$ is least. The least distance from the origin to $L$ occurs when $OP\perp L$. (D) is true.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pole-polar and inversion: the chord of contact is the polar of $P$, the midpoint of $AB$ is the inverse of $P$ in the circle, and the circumcentre is the midpoint of $OP$.
solution: The polars of all points of a line pass through the pole of that line. The pole of $3x+4y=25$ w.r.t. $x^2+y^2=4$ is $\left(\frac{4\cdot3}{25},\frac{4\cdot4}{25}\right)=\left(\frac{12}{25},\frac{16}{25}\right)$. (A) true.
The circumcentre of $\triangle PAB$ is the midpoint of $OP$ (diameter $OP$). The homothety with centre $O$ and ratio $\frac12$ maps $3x+4y=25$ to $3x+4y=\frac{25}{2}$, i.e. $6x+8y=25$. (B) true.
In right triangle $OAP$ with altitude $AN$, $OA^2=ON\cdot OP$, so $ON\cdot OP=4$: the midpoint $N$ of $AB$ is the inverse of $P$ in the circle.

The inverse of a line not through $O$ is a circle through $O$. The foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $L$ is at distance $5$ along $\left(\frac35,\frac45\right)$; its inverse is at distance $\frac45$, i.e. the point $\left(\frac{12}{25},\frac{16}{25}\right)$. The locus is the circle with diameter from $O$ to that point: $x^2+y^2-\frac{12}{25}x-\frac{16}{25}y=0$. (C) true.
$ON=\frac4d$, so $AB=2\sqrt{4-ON^2}=4\sqrt{1-\frac4{d^2}}$, increasing in $d=OP$. It is least for the least $OP$, i.e. $OP\perp L$. (D) true.

useful_results: The chord of contact (polar) of every point of a line passes through the pole of that line. The pole of $lx+my=n$ w.r.t. $x^2+y^2=r^2$ is $\left(\frac{lr^2}{n},\frac{mr^2}{n}\right)$.
$O,A,P,B$ are concyclic with diameter $OP$, so the circumcentre of $\triangle PAB$ is the midpoint of $OP$.
The midpoint $N$ of the chord of contact satisfies $ON\cdot OP=r^2$ (inverse of $P$). The locus of $N$ as $P$ moves on a line not through $O$ is a circle through $O$.
$AB=\frac{2r\sqrt{d^2-r^2}}{d}$ increases with $d=OP$. Here $d_{\min}=5$ gives $AB_{\min}=\frac{4\sqrt{21}}{5}\approx3.67$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Limit of a function defined through $x^{2n}$; differentiability and higher derivatives
Lagrange's mean value theorem
questions.question: Consider the function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{x^{2n}(x^4-2x^2+2)+(\cos(\pi x)+2)}{x^{2n}+1}$. Which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The function $f(x)$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$, but its second derivative $f''(x)$ does not exist at $x=1$ and $x=-1$.
According to Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem applied to $f(x)$ on the interval $[0,2]$, there exists a unique $c\in(0,2)$ such that $f'(c)=\frac72$, and this $c$ lies in the subinterval $(1,2)$.
The number of points $c\in(-2,2)$ satisfying $f'(c)=0$ is exactly $3$.
questions.key_idea: $x^{2n}\to0,\infty$ splits $f$ into $\cos\pi x+2$ and $x^4-2x^2+2$; the join at $\pm1$ is $C^1$ but not $C^2$.
solution: For $|x|<1$, $x^{2n}\to0$; for $|x|>1$, $x^{2n}\to\infty$; at $x=\pm1$ the limit is $\frac{(1-2+2)+(\cos\pi+2)}{2}=1$. So $f(x)=\cos\pi x+2$ for $|x|<1$; $x^4-2x^2+2$ for $|x|>1$; $1$ for $x=\pm1$.
Continuity at $x=1$: $\lim_{x\to1^-}f(x)=\cos\pi+2=1$ and $\lim_{x\to1^+}f(x)=1-2+2=1$. Since $f(1)=1$, $f$ is continuous.
Thus $f'(1)=0$; by symmetry ($f$ is even) $f'(-1)=0$. Hence $f$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$.
Since $\pi^2\neq8$, $f''(1)$ does not exist; by symmetry neither does $f''(-1)$. (A) is true.
$f$ is continuous on $[0,2]$ and differentiable on $(0,2)$, so Lagrange's MVT gives some $c\in(0,2)$ with $f'(c)=\frac{f(2)-f(0)}{2}=\frac{10-3}{2}=\frac72$.
On $(0,1)$, $f'(x)=-\pi\sin\pi x<0$, so $f'(c)=\frac72$ has no solution there. For $c\ge1$: $4c^3-4c=\frac72\Rightarrow8c^3-8c-7=0$. Let $h(x)=8x^3-8x-7$: $h(1)=-7<0$ and $h(2)=41>0$.
$h'(x)=24x^2-8>0$ for $x>1$, so $h$ is strictly increasing there. Thus a unique root exists, and it lies in $(1,2)$. (C) is true.
The solutions are exactly $\{-1,0,1\}$, i.e. exactly $3$ points. (D) is true. So (A), (B), (C), (D) are all true.
questions.correction_note: Statement (C): the PDF proves a unique root of $8c^3-8c-7=0$ in $(1,2)$ but never rules out $c\in(0,1)$, which the claim 'unique $c\in(0,2)$' needs. Added: on $(0,1)$ $f'(x)=-\pi\sin\pi x<0\neq\frac72$. All results and the answer (A, B, C, D) are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Local expansion at the join: $f-1\approx\frac{\pi^2}{2}h^2$ on the left and $4h^2$ on the right of $x=1$, so $f\in C^1$ but $f''$ jumps.
solution: Both sides are $O(h^2)$: $f(1)=1$ and $f'(1)=0$ from both sides, so $f$ is differentiable at $\pm1$.
Since $f-1\approx\frac{f''}{2}h^2$ on each side, the one-sided second derivatives are $\pi^2$ and $8$: unequal, so $f''(\pm1)$ does not exist. (A) true.

$f'$ is continuous; $f'=-\pi\sin\pi x\le0$ on $[0,1]$ and $f'=4x(x^2-1)$ on $[1,2]$ is strictly increasing from $0$ to $f'(2)=24$ (as $f''=12x^2-4>0$). So $f'=\frac72$ happens only in $(1,2)$, exactly once. (C) true.
$f'$ is odd. On $(0,2)$ its only zero is $x=1$ ($f'<0$ on $(0,1)$, $f'>0$ on $(1,2)$); with $x=0$ and, by oddness, $x=-1$, the zeros are $-1,0,1$. (D) true.

useful_results: For $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{x^{2n}A(x)+B(x)}{x^{2n}+1}$: the limit is $B$ for $|x|<1$, $A$ for $|x|>1$ and $\frac{A+B}{2}$ for $|x|=1$.
At a join where two pieces agree in value and in slope, $f''$ exists iff the second derivatives of the two pieces also agree there. Here $\pi^2$ vs $8$.
Coefficient extraction: $\frac{\cos\pi x-1+\frac{\pi^2x^2}{2}}{x^4}\to\frac{\pi^4}{24}$ (the coefficient of $x^4$ in $\cos\pi x$).
A value $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ is taken by $f'$ exactly once on any interval where $f'$ is strictly monotone. Locate the right subinterval from the sign of $f'$ first.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Leibniz rule for definite integrals with symmetric limits
Monotonicity, odd functions and limits
questions.question: Consider the function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=\int_{-x}^{x}\frac{t^2+\cos t}{1+e^t}\,dt$. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
options: $f(x)$ is a strictly increasing function on $\mathbb{R}$.
questions.key_idea: Differentiating with limits $\pm x$ pairs $\frac1{1+e^x}$ with $\frac1{1+e^{-x}}$, and these add up to $1$.
solution: $x^2+\cos x>0$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$ ($\cos x>0$ for $|x|<1$, and $x^2\ge1$ with $x^2+\cos x\ge 1+\cos 1>0$ for $|x|\ge1$), so $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$. (A) is true.
Clearly $f(-x)=-f(x)$, so $f(x)$ is an odd function. (B) is true.

alternate_solutions.idea: For even $h$, $\int_{-a}^{a}\frac{h(t)}{1+e^t}dt=\int_0^a h(t)\,dt$: no differentiation of the integral is needed.
solution: So $f$ is odd (B), $f(\pi)=\frac{\pi^3}{3}$ (C), $f'(x)=x^2+\cos x>0$ (A), and $\frac{f(x)}{x}\to1\neq0$ (D false).

useful_results: For even $h$ and $k>0$: $\int_{-a}^{a}\frac{h(t)}{1+k^t}dt=\int_0^ah(t)\,dt$ (the king/pairing trick).
Leibniz rule: $\frac{d}{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}\phi(t)\,dt=\phi(v)\,v'-\phi(u)\,u'$.
If $f(x)=\int_{-x}^{x}\phi(t)\,dt$ with $\phi$ continuous, then $f$ is odd and $f'(x)=\phi(x)+\phi(-x)$; $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f(x)}{x}=f'(0)$. Here $f'(0)=0^2+\cos0=1$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Determinants
Derivatives of an inverse function
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function defined by $f(x)=\left|\begin{matrix}x&1&1\\-1&x&1\\-1&-1&x\end{matrix}\right|$. Let $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be the inverse function of $f(x)$. Consider the function $D(x)$ defined by the determinant $D(x)=\left|\begin{matrix}g(x)&1&0\\g'(x)&g(x)&1\\g''(x)&g'(x)&g(x)\end{matrix}\right|$. Which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
solution: $f'(x)=3x^2+3>0$ for all $x$, so $f$ is strictly increasing, hence bijective, and the inverse function $g$ exists.
To find $g(4)$ set $f(x)=4$: $x^3+3x=4$ has the unique real root $x=1$. Hence $g(4)=1$.
At $x=1$: $g''(4)=-\frac{6}{6^3}=-\frac{1}{36}$. So (B), which claims $-\frac1{72}$, is false.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write every derivative of $g$ in the variable $s=g(y)$, using $\frac{d}{dy}=\frac{1}{3(s^2+1)}\frac{d}{ds}$, so $D$ becomes a function of $s$ alone.
solution: Let $y=s^3+3s$, so $g(y)=s$ and $\frac{d}{dy}=\frac{1}{3(s^2+1)}\frac{d}{ds}$. The point $y=4$ corresponds to $s=1$.

useful_results: Derivatives of an inverse at $y_0=f(x_0)$: $g'=\frac1{f'}$, $g''=-\frac{f''}{f'^3}$, $g'''=\frac{3f''^2-f'f'''}{f'^5}$, all evaluated at $x_0$.
Find $f^{-1}(y_0)$ by inspection when $f$ is strictly increasing: $x^3+3x=4\Rightarrow x=1$, unique.
$\left|\begin{matrix}a&1&0\\b&a&1\\c&b&a\end{matrix}\right|=a^3-2ab+c$ (check: $a(a^2-b)-(ab-c)$). With $a=g$, $b=g'$, $c=g''$.
A $3\times3$ determinant with a row/column pattern of $\pm1$ often reduces to a cubic: $\left|\begin{matrix}x&1&1\\-1&x&1\\-1&-1&x\end{matrix}\right|=x^3+3x$.

concepts: Parametric differentiation and second derivative
questions.paragraph: Consider a curve $C$ defined parametrically for $t>0$ by the equations $x(t)=\ln(t^2+1)-\frac{t^2}{t^2+1}$ and $y(t)=\frac{t^4}{4}-t^2+\frac32\ln(t^2+1)+\frac{1}{2(t^2+1)}$. Let $f(x)$ denote the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at any point $(x,y)$.
questions.question: The value of $\frac{df}{dx}$ at the point on the curve where the tangent is parallel to the line $2y-x=5$ is
questions.key_idea: Treat the slope $f$ as a function of $t$ and differentiate again by the chain rule: $\frac{df}{dx}=\frac{df/dt}{dx/dt}$.
solution: The tangent is parallel to $2y-x=5$, so the slope is $\frac12$: $\frac{t^4}{2}=\frac12\Rightarrow t=1$ (since $t>0$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the standard formula $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{x'y''-y'x''}{(x')^3}$ at $t=1$ without simplifying $f$.

useful_results: For $x=x(t)$, $y=y(t)$: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y'}{x'}$ and $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{x'y''-y'x''}{(x')^3}$. Since $f=\frac{dy}{dx}$, $\frac{df}{dx}=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$.
Such parametrisations are built so that $x'$ and $y'$ factor nicely (here $\frac{2t^3}{(t^2+1)^2}$ and $\frac{t^7}{(t^2+1)^2}$); simplify before taking ratios.
A tangent parallel to $ax+by=c$ has slope $-\frac ab$.

concepts: Parametric differentiation
Monotonicity of a function
questions.paragraph: Consider a curve $C$ defined parametrically for $t>0$ by the equations $x(t)=\ln(t^2+1)-\frac{t^2}{t^2+1}$ and $y(t)=\frac{t^4}{4}-t^2+\frac32\ln(t^2+1)+\frac{1}{2(t^2+1)}$. Let $f(x)$ denote the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at any point $(x,y)$.
questions.question: If $g(x)=f(x)-(e^2)x$, then the interval in which $g(x)$ is strictly increasing is
questions.key_idea: $x(t)$ is increasing, so the condition $t>t_0$ turns into $x>x(t_0)$.
solution: For $g(x)$ to be strictly increasing we need $\frac{dg}{dx}>0$: $(t^2+1)^2-e^2>0\Rightarrow t^2+1>e\Rightarrow t>\sqrt{e-1}$.
Since $\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{2t^3}{(t^2+1)^2}>0$ for all $t>0$, $x(t)$ is a strictly increasing function.
Hence $g(x)$ is strictly increasing for $x\in\left(\frac1e,\infty\right)$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Take $s=t^2+1$ as the parameter: $x=\ln s+\frac1s-1$ and the condition becomes simply $s>e$.
solution: At $s=e$: $x=1+\frac1e-1=\frac1e$. So $g$ increases exactly for $x>\frac1e$: option (C).

useful_results: If $x(t)$ is strictly increasing, intervals in $t$ map to intervals in $x$ with the same order; only the endpoint value $x(t_0)$ has to be computed.
$g(x)=f(x)-cx$ is increasing exactly where $f'(x)>c$; here $f'(x)=(t^2+1)^2$ grows with $t$, giving a single threshold $t^2+1=\sqrt c=e$.
When $t^2+1$ appears repeatedly, use $s=t^2+1$ as the parameter; $x(s)=\ln s+\frac1s-1$ is increasing for $s>1$.

concepts: Implicit differentiation and second derivative
questions.question: Consider a real-valued function $y=f(x)$ defined implicitly by the equation $y^2+\sin(xy)+x=y$ in a neighborhood of $x=0$ such that $f(0)=0$. If $f''(0)$ denotes the second-order derivative of $f(x)$ at $x=0$, then the value of $f''(0)$ is
questions.key_idea: Differentiate implicitly twice and put $x=y=0$: every $\sin(xy)$ term vanishes, leaving $2y'^2+2y'=y''$.
solution: Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$: $2yy'+\cos(xy)(y+xy')+1=y'$.
Differentiating once more with respect to $x$: $2(y')^2+2yy''-\sin(xy)(y+xy')^2+\cos(xy)(2y'+xy'')=y''$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Assume $y=ax+bx^2+\dots$ and compare coefficients (Maclaurin series); then $y''(0)=2b$.

useful_results: For $F(x,y)=0$ through $(0,0)$, put $y=ax+bx^2+\dots$ and match powers of $x$: then $y'(0)=a$, $y''(0)=2b$, with no repeated differentiation.
$\sin(xy)=xy+O(x^3y^3)$, so near the origin $\sin(xy)$ contributes only from order $x^2$ (here $ax^2$).
Second implicit derivative: differentiate the first relation once more (product and chain rule) and substitute the known point and $y'$; no need to solve for $y'$ in general.

concepts: Greatest integer and fractional part functions
Limit of the $1^\infty$ form
questions.question: Let $[t]$ and $\{t\}$ denote the greatest integer function and fractional part function of $t$, respectively. For $x\in(0,1)\setminus\left\{\frac1n:n\in\mathbb{N}\right\}$, consider the real-valued functions $\Phi(x)=\frac{1-x^2\left[\frac1x\right]^2-x^2\left\{\frac1x\right\}^2}{2x\left[\frac1x\right]}$ and $\Psi(x)=\frac{\left\{\frac1x\right\}}{\left[\frac1x\right]+\left\{\frac1x\right\}}$. If $L=\lim_{x\to0^+}\left(\frac{2^{\Phi(x)}+8^{\Phi(x)}+32^{\Phi(x)}}{3}\right)^{\frac{1}{\Psi(x)}}$, then the value of $L$ is
questions.key_idea: $y^2=[y]^2+\{y\}^2+2[y]\{y\}$ shows $\Phi=\Psi=x\{\frac1x\}\to0^+$, so $L$ is a $1^\infty$ limit in one variable $u$.
solution: For $x\in(0,1)\setminus\left\{\frac1n\right\}$: $0<\left\{\frac1x\right\}<1\Rightarrow0<x\left\{\frac1x\right\}<x$. By the Squeeze Theorem, $u=x\left\{\frac1x\right\}\to0^+$ as $x\to0^+$.

Substituting $u=\Phi(x)=\Psi(x)$: $L=\lim_{u\to0^+}\left(\frac{2^u+8^u+32^u}{3}\right)^{\frac1u}$, an indeterminate form $1^\infty$. Taking the natural logarithm: $\ln L=\lim_{u\to0^+}\frac1u\ln\left(1+\frac{(2^u-1)+(8^u-1)+(32^u-1)}{3}\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Recognise the limit as a power mean: $\left(\frac{a^u+b^u+c^u}{3}\right)^{1/u}\to\sqrt[3]{abc}$ as $u\to0$, and read $2,8,32$ as $2^1,2^3,2^5$.
solution: As above, $\Phi=\Psi=u=x\left\{\frac1x\right\}\in(0,x)$, so $u\to0^+$ and $L=\lim_{u\to0^+}M_u(2,8,32)$, where $M_u(a,b,c)=\left(\frac{a^u+b^u+c^u}{3}\right)^{1/u}$ is the power mean of order $u$.
As $u\to0$ the power mean tends to the geometric mean: $M_u\to\sqrt[3]{abc}$.

useful_results: As $x\to0^+$: $x\left\{\frac1x\right\}\in(0,x)\to0^+$, whereas $x\left[\frac1x\right]\to1^-$ (since $1-x<x\left[\frac1x\right]\le1$).
Power mean limit: $\lim_{u\to0}\left(\frac{a_1^u+\dots+a_n^u}{n}\right)^{1/u}=\left(a_1\cdots a_n\right)^{1/n}$ for $a_i>0$.
$1^\infty$ form: $\lim(1+h)^{1/u}=e^{\lim h/u}$ when $h\to0$; and $\lim_{u\to0}\frac{a^u-1}{u}=\ln a$.

concepts: Integration of $e^x(u+u')$ and of the form $v+xv'$
Monotonicity and derivative of a function
questions.question: Let $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function defined by $f(x)=\int e^x\left(\frac{x^2-x+1}{(x^2+1)^{3/2}}\right)dx+\int\frac{x^2+1+(1-x^2)\ln x}{(x^2+1)^2}\,dx$ such that $f(1)=\frac{e}{\sqrt2}+2$. Consider the function $g:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $g(x)=(x^2+1)f(x)-e^x\sqrt{x^2+1}$. If $g(x)$ is strictly increasing at $x=\frac12$ and $g'\left(\frac12\right)=k-\ln2$, then the value of the integer $k$ is
questions.key_idea: Spot $e^x(u+u')$ with $u=\frac1{\sqrt{x^2+1}}$ and $v+xv'=(xv)'$ with $v=\frac{\ln x}{x^2+1}$; then $g$ collapses to $x\ln x+2x^2+2$.
solution: The integrand can be written as $e^x\left(u(x)+u'(x)\right)=e^x\frac{x^2-x+1}{(x^2+1)^{3/2}}$, so the first integral is $\frac{e^x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}$.
Second integral: let $v(x)=\frac{\ln x}{x^2+1}$, so $v'(x)=\frac{x^2+1-2x^2\ln x}{x(x^2+1)^2}$.
The integrand matches the form $v(x)+xv'(x)=\frac{x^2+1+(1-x^2)\ln x}{(x^2+1)^2}$, so the second integral is $x\,v(x)=\frac{x\ln x}{x^2+1}$.
Since $3-\ln2>0$, $g(x)$ is strictly increasing at $x=\frac12$. Comparing $g'\left(\frac12\right)=3-\ln2$ with $k-\ln2$ gives $k=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Integrate by parts instead of recognising the forms: $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{x^2+1}=\frac{1-x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\frac1{\sqrt{x^2+1}}=-\frac{x}{(x^2+1)^{3/2}}$.
solution: By parts, $\int\ln x\,d\left(\frac{x}{x^2+1}\right)=\frac{x\ln x}{x^2+1}-\int\frac{1}{x^2+1}dx$. Adding $\int\frac{dx}{x^2+1}$ leaves $\frac{x\ln x}{x^2+1}$.

useful_results: $\int e^x\left(u+u'\right)dx=e^xu$. Look for $u$ whose derivative produces the extra term (here $u=(x^2+1)^{-1/2}$).
$\int\left(v+xv'\right)dx=xv$ (product rule). More generally $\int\left(v\,w'+v'w\right)dx=vw$.
$\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{x^2+1}=\frac{1-x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}=-\frac{x}{(x^2+1)^{3/2}}$ - standard building blocks for such integrands.
When $g$ is built from an antiderivative, expect heavy cancellation: simplify $g$ before differentiating (here $g=x\ln x+2x^2+2$).

concepts: Distance between parallel lines and a circle touching two lines
Pole and polar (chord of contact) of a circle
questions.question: Consider two parallel lines $L_1:3x-4y+7=0$ and $L_2:3x-4y-3=0$ in the $xy$-plane. A circle $C$ is inscribed between $L_1$ and $L_2$ such that it is tangent to both lines. Let $L_3$ be another line parallel to $L_1$ and distinct from $L_2$, such that the distance between $L_1$ and $L_3$ is equal to the distance between $L_1$ and $L_2$. From a variable point $P$ on the line $L_3$, a pair of tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn to the circle $C$, where $A$ and $B$ are the points of contact. As $P$ varies along $L_3$, the chord of contact $AB$ always passes through a fixed point $Q$. If $d_1$ and $d_2$ denote the perpendicular distances of the point $Q$ from the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively, then the value of the ratio $\frac{d_2}{d_1}$ is
questions.key_idea: The lines are $2$ apart, so $R=1$ and $L_3$ is $3$ from the centre; the fixed point is the pole of $L_3$, at distance $\frac{R^2}{3}=\frac13$ from the centre.
solution: Distance between the parallel lines $L_1$ and $L_2$: $\frac{|7-(-3)|}{\sqrt{3^2+(-4)^2}}=\frac{10}{5}=2$.
Since the circle $C$ is tangent to both lines, its diameter is $2$, so the radius is $R=1$.
The centre of the circle lies on the midline of $L_1$ and $L_2$: $3x-4y+2=0$.
$L_3$ is parallel to $L_1$ at a distance of $2$ units. Since $L_3\neq L_2$, its equation must be $3x-4y+7+10=0\Rightarrow3x-4y+17=0$.
Project the geometry on an axis perpendicular to the lines, taking the centre of the circle as origin $O$. The positions along this axis are: centre $=0$, $L_2=-1$, $L_1=+1$, $L_3=+3$.
The variable point $P$ lies on $L_3$, so the chord of contact $AB$ always passes through the pole of the line $L_3$ with respect to the circle $C$. The distance of $L_3$ from the centre is $d=3$.

By the properties of poles and polars, the fixed point $Q$ (the pole) lies on the same perpendicular axis at $OQ=\frac{R^2}{d}=\frac{1^2}{3}=\frac13$. So the position of $Q$ on this axis is $+\frac13$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coordinates adapted to the lines: the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ between the lines $y=\pm1$, and the chord of contact written as $T=0$ for a general point of $L_3:y=3$.
solution: Choose axes with $C:x^2+y^2=1$, $L_1:y=1$, $L_2:y=-1$ and $L_3:y=3$ (on the $L_1$ side, since $L_3\neq L_2$).
For $P=(p,3)$ on $L_3$, the chord of contact $T=0$ is $px+3y=1$.
For every $p$ this line passes through $Q=\left(0,\frac13\right)$, because $p\cdot0+3\cdot\frac13=1$. So $Q$ is fixed.

useful_results: For points $P$ moving on a line at distance $d$ from the centre of a circle of radius $R$, the chord of contact always passes through the pole of that line, at distance $\frac{R^2}{d}$ from the centre on the perpendicular from the centre to the line.
A circle tangent to two parallel lines at distance $w$ has $R=\frac w2$ and its centre on the midline.
Choosing an axis along the common normal of parallel lines turns a slanted two-dimensional problem into a one-dimensional one.

concepts: Non-differentiability of $\max$ and $\min$ of functions
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function defined by $f(x)=\max\left\{x,\ \min\left\{x^2,\ 2-x^2\right\}\right\}$. If $N$ is the number of points in $\mathbb{R}$ where $f(x)$ is not differentiable, then the value of $N$ is
questions.key_idea: Find where the active branch of the $\max/\min$ changes (crossings of $x$, $x^2$, $2-x^2$) and test whether the slopes agree there.
solution: Hence $f(x)=\begin{cases}x, & x\le-2\\ 2-x^2, & -2<x\le-1\\ x^2, & -1<x\le0\\ x, & x>0\end{cases}$ and $f(x)$ is continuous everywhere.
Differentiating in each interval: $f'(x)=\begin{cases}1, & x<-2\\ -2x, & -2<x<-1\\ 2x, & -1<x<0\\ 1, & x>0\end{cases}$
At $x=-2$: LHD $=1$, RHD $=4$, not differentiable. At $x=-1$: LHD $=2$, RHD $=-2$, not differentiable. At $x=0$: LHD $=0$, RHD $=1$, not differentiable.
Thus $f(x)$ is non-differentiable at exactly $3$ points ($x=-2,-1,0$). Hence $N=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Graph view: sketch $y=x$, $y=x^2$, $y=2-x^2$ and look only at crossings where the curve that forms $f$ actually switches.
solution: The three curves cross at $x=-2$ ($x=2-x^2$), $x=\pm1$ ($x^2=2-x^2$), $x=0$ and $x=1$ ($x=x^2$); at $x=1$ all three meet at $(1,1)$.
A max/min of smooth functions can fail to be differentiable only at a crossing where the function that forms $f$ switches from one curve to another.
$x=1$: $f=x$ on both sides (the lower envelope $g$ switches but stays below $x$), so there is no corner.

$x=0$: $f$ switches from $x^2$ to $x$ (slopes $0$ and $1$): a corner. $x=-1$: $f$ switches from $2-x^2$ to $x^2$ (slopes $2$ and $-2$): a corner. $x=-2$: $f$ switches from $x$ to $2-x^2$ (slopes $1$ and $4$): a corner.

useful_results: $\max\{a,b\}=\frac{a+b+|a-b|}{2}$ and $\min\{a,b\}=\frac{a+b-|a-b|}{2}$: non-differentiability can arise only where $a=b$ and $a'\neq b'$.
If the active function does not switch at a crossing (the third curve stays on top or bottom), there is no corner. Here $x=1$.
Count candidates systematically: solve $x=x^2$, $x=2-x^2$, $x^2=2-x^2$ and keep only the crossings that lie on the envelope with unequal slopes.

concepts: Point of inflection and angle between two curves
questions.question: Consider the function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=2x^3-6x^2+4x$. Let $P(x_0,y_0)$ be the point on the curve $y=f(x)$ where the curve changes its concavity. Let $C$ be another curve defined by $y=\ln(2x-1)$ for $x>\frac12$. If $\theta$ is the acute angle of intersection between the curve $y=f(x)$ and the curve $C$ at the point $P$, then the value of $3\tan\theta$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: The inflection point is where $f''$ changes sign; the angle between curves is the angle between their tangents, $\tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|$.
solution: The curve changes its concavity where $f''(x)$ changes sign, which occurs uniquely at $x=1$. There $y=f(1)=2-6+4=0$.
For $C:y=\ln(2x-1)$, $x=1$ gives $y=\ln1=0$, which confirms that $P(1,0)$ is a point of intersection of both curves.
Slope of the tangent to the first curve at $P$: $m_1=f'(1)=6(1)^2-12(1)+4=-2$.
For $C$: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{2x-1}$, so the slope of the tangent at $P(1,0)$ is $m_2=\frac{2}{2(1)-1}=2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use direction vectors of the two tangents and the dot product instead of the slope formula.
solution: $\cos\varphi=\frac{(1)(1)+(-2)(2)}{\sqrt5\,\sqrt5}=-\frac35$, so the angle between the vectors is obtuse; the acute angle $\theta$ has $\cos\theta=\frac35$.

useful_results: Angle between curves at a common point = angle between their tangents: $\tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|$; equivalently $\cos\theta=\frac{|1+m_1m_2|}{\sqrt{(1+m_1^2)(1+m_2^2)}}$. The curves are orthogonal iff $m_1m_2=-1$.
The cubic $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ has a unique inflection point at $x=-\frac{b}{3a}$ (here $x=1$), and it is the centre of symmetry of the curve.
Always verify that the common point lies on both curves ($\ln(2\cdot1-1)=0$) before using tangent slopes there.

concepts: Tangents from an external point; area of quadrilateral $CAPB$ and shortest distance from a line
questions.question: Consider the circle $x^2+y^2-4x-6y-12=0$ and the straight line $3x+4y=83$. Let $P$ be a variable point on this straight line. Two tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn to the circle, where $A$ and $B$ are the points of tangency. Let $C$ denote the center of the circle. If the minimum area of the quadrilateral $CAPB$ is $\Delta$, then the value of $\Delta$ is
questions.key_idea: Area $=R\cdot AP=R\sqrt{CP^2-R^2}$ increases with $CP$, so it is least when $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to the line.
solution: The circle $x^2+y^2-4x-6y-12=0$ has centre $C(2,3)$ and radius $R=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-3)^2-(-12)}=\sqrt{4+9+12}=5$.
The perpendicular distance from $C(2,3)$ to the line $3x+4y-83=0$ is the shortest distance from $C$ to the line: $d=\frac{|3(2)+4(3)-83|}{\sqrt{3^2+4^2}}=\frac{|6+12-83|}{5}=\frac{65}{5}=13$.

The quadrilateral $CAPB$ is formed by two congruent right-angled triangles $CAP$ and $CBP$ (right angles at $A$ and $B$). So the area is $2\times\left(\frac12\times CA\times AP\right)=R\times L$, where $L=AP$ is the tangent length.
From the right triangle $CAP$: $L=\sqrt{CP^2-R^2}=\sqrt{CP^2-25}$. Thus the area is $5\sqrt{CP^2-25}$.
To minimise the area, $CP$ must be minimised. The minimum value of $CP$ is the perpendicular distance $d=13$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise $P$ on the line and minimise the power $S_{11}$ of $P$ w.r.t. the circle, a quadratic in one variable.
solution: Area $=R\,L=5\sqrt{S_{11}}$, where $S_{11}=x^2+y^2-4x-6y-12$ is the power of $P(x,y)$ w.r.t. the circle.
On the line, $y=\frac{83-3x}{4}$, so $S_{11}$ becomes a quadratic in $x$ with positive leading coefficient $1+\frac9{16}=\frac{25}{16}$.
It is least at its vertex, where $\frac{dS_{11}}{dx}=0$: $x=\frac{49}{5}$, so $y=\frac{83-\frac{147}{5}}{4}=\frac{67}{5}$ (the foot of the perpendicular from $C$).

useful_results: For tangents $PA,PB$ from $P$ to a circle with centre $C$, radius $R$: $AP=\sqrt{CP^2-R^2}$, area of $CAPB=R\sqrt{CP^2-R^2}$ and $AB=\frac{2R\sqrt{CP^2-R^2}}{CP}$.
For $P$ moving on a line, tangent length, area of $CAPB$ and chord $AB$ all increase with $CP$ (and $\angle APB$ decreases), so each optimum is at the foot of the perpendicular from $C$.
Recognise Pythagorean triples: $R=5$, $CP=13$ gives $AP=12$ at once ($5$-$12$-$13$).
Distance from $(x_1,y_1)$ to $ax+by+c=0$ is $\frac{|ax_1+by_1+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$.
